articles.summary: Business Center How Do You Know If Your Business Is Ready to Scale? Oluwakemi Adesina September 22, 2026 Every founder dreams of growth, but what sets forward-thinking founders apart is that they plan for the capacity to carry it, well ahead of time. Growth can bring more customers, more revenue, bigger contracts and access to markets that once seemed out of reach. But growth also puts weight on every system underneath the business. The processes that felt perfectly adequate at 15 employees can buckle at 100. Financial records that worked with three revenue streams can become impossible to defend when a lender asks for a clear picture of margins. The informal way a founder managed people can collapse when the organisation becomes too large for everyone to know everyone else. That is the real test of growth, and it is normal. Think of it as a coming-of-age phase for every business, survivable by only the most resilient of businesses. Businesses that scale successfully in Nigeria’s changing economy are not necessarily the ones with the fewest problems. They also faced the myriad of problems Nigerian businesses face, but the defining thing about them, is that they identified the weaknesses that will come with their growth early and took care of those weaknesses before it grounded their business. At Eazipay, we see those weaknesses repeatedly across businesses at different stages of growth. They tend to concentrate in three areas: people infrastructure, cost structure and compliance framework. That’s why we call them the Three Growth Tests. So, if your business plans to hire significantly, serve more customers, raise capital, enter new markets or take on larger contracts, these are three areas worth testing before the next stage arrives. Get your results in 3 minutes Why readiness matters now For years, Nigerian businesses have had to spend significant management attention solving problems that had little to do with building the business itself. Founders navigated unpredictable foreign exchange access. Businesses worked around transaction limits. Cross-border payments created friction. Infrastructure problems raised operating costs. Teams stretched themselves across functions because building a fully staffed organisation was often harder than finding another workaround. So businesses adapted. They found alternative payment routes. They created manual processes. They kept records in different places. They asked one person to handle three functions because hiring three specialists did not make economic sense yet. Those adaptations helped keep businesses in motion. But they also created a habit that can become dangerous during the next phase of growth: solving each new problem as it appears instead of building a structure that prevents the same class of problems from returning. That distinction matters more as Nigeria’s business environment changes. In October 2025, the Financial Action Task Force removed Nigeria from its Grey List of jurisdictions under increased monitoring after concluding that Nigeria had completed the required action plan. The European Union subsequently removed Nigeria from its list of high-risk third countries through a regulation published in January 2026. Just around the same time, Nigeria’s new Tax Administration Act also took effect, introducing a new framework for tax administration and collection. These changes may seem unconnected, but they are. And while they all begin at the policy level, businesses experience them through practical questions. How easily can money move? How prepared are you to work with larger financial institutions? Can you satisfy the documentation requirements of a major customer? Can you produce reliable financial records when someone wants to invest or lend? Can your business handle a larger volume of transactions without creating new compliance problems? These questions are pertinent to the survival of your business as they determine how ready you are to meet the significant opportunity presented by these policy changes. These changes will bring about a more connected economy, and a more connected economy can give Nigerian businesses access to more customers, more capital, more trade and more opportunities to compete beyond the domestic market. But there’s a bigger catch. This opportunity also raises the standard your business must meet. That you have more room to grow is not the same as having the capacity to grow. That is where our Three Growth Tests come in. The first Growth Test: Is your people infrastructure ready? Early-stage businesses often run on adaptable generalists. That can be a strength, because when a company has ten or fifteen people, flexibility allows everyone to move quickly. The founder can step into recruitment when someone resigns, help finance when a payment needs approval and sit with operations when a customer issue needs solving. The business works because the people inside it compensate for the gaps in the structure. However, growth changes that equation. As headcount increases, the company needs more than hardworking people. It needs clarity about who owns what, how decisions get made and how the organisation develops and manages its people. That is what people infrastructure should provide. A strong people infrastructure gives the business: Clear job responsibilities and decision rights Defined performance expectations Consistent performance management and feedback Training, mentorship and leadership development Reliable workforce data for management decisions Structured payroll and employee administration Proper handling of applicable statutory obligations and benefits Systems that reduce unnecessary manual work The exact structure should match the business. That means a 15-person company does not need the same HR infrastructure as a 150-person organisation. But even then, the principle remains the same: the company needs to increase its ability to manage people at roughly the same pace it increases the number of people it employs. There’s another point to note here, which is that growth changes the kind of people you need. So, how does that happen? Why growth changes the kind of people you need Founders often underestimate the fact that growth does not simply require more people. It often requires different capabilities. articles.summary: Second PMDA approval for Signatera in three months and first PMDA-approved CDx in MRD-guided care; commercial launch expected in 1H’27, pending final reimbursement and pricing Natera, Inc. (NASDAQ: NTRA), a global leader in cell-free DNA and precision medicine, today announced that its Signatera test has received regulatory approval from Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) as a companion diagnostic (CDx) in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). This approval supports the use of the Signatera test to guide adjuvant atezolizumab (Tecentriq®) treatment decisions in patients with MIBC. Natera expects to commercially launch Signatera for MIBC in Japan in the first half of 2027, following the PMDA’s approval of atezolizumab in MIBC. Regulatory approval was supported by data from IMvigor011, a randomized, double-blind phase III clinical trial that evaluated Signatera-guided adjuvant atezolizumab in patients with MIBC. The trial included more than 20 participating sites
articles.title: Signatera™ Receives Regulatory Approval in Japan as a Companion Diagnostic in Muscle-Invasive Bladder Cancer
